![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14133254/assets/1fca2d0c37c8831a66c3c183b31b84b41fd5a16740ff13fd86f4877bdaeb60a6.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
question.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ we obtain $r=2.$

- For $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =1 \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ r & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(1,\sqrt{3}).$ So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14133254/assets/1060c071df1dbd197c14da529819a34bd4457868fdd4cbe78a7f93f12dbf67da.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{4x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [r]_{\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (2-\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -4\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =[(8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\frac{4\pi }{3})-0] \\  & =4\sqrt{3}-\frac{4\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
